questions.prompt: History: C0←C1←C2←C3 on main; feature branches from C1 with C4←C5. How many commits is main ahead of feature? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: C2 and C3 are on main only.

questions.prompt: History: C0←C1←C2←C3 on main; feature branches from C1 with C4←C5. What is the generation number (1 for a root) of C5? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
`git merge feature` is run while on main, and main's tip is an ancestor of feature's tip. What happens by default?
options: The merge is refused because main has no new commits of its own
main's label moves forward (fast-forward); no merge commit is created
A merge commit with two parents is always created, even without divergence
All commits of main are rewritten on top of feature's tip
questions.explanation: When no divergence exists, Git just advances the label.

questions.prompt: What happens to a commit's id if you change only its message with `git commit --amend`?
options: A new commit with a different id replaces it; its descendants must be rewritten too
The id changes only if the files changed, since the id hashes the tree
The id stays the same because the message is stored separately from the content
Only the message object changes, and the commit id is kept for the parents
questions.explanation: The message is part of the hashed content; amending creates a new commit.

questions.prompt: A Git blob object for a 6-byte file starts with the header text 'blob 6', then a NUL byte, then the content. How many characters long is that header text? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: 'blob 6' is 6 characters; the object is that, a NUL byte and the 6 content bytes.

questions.prompt: A diff hunk header reads @@ -10,6 +10,9 @@. How many more lines does the new file have in this hunk? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
A diff shows every line of a file as changed although you only edited one line. A likely cause?
options: The branch was fast-forwarded
Line endings were converted (CRLF/LF)
Git stores whole files for every commit
The file has too many lines
questions.explanation: Different line endings make every line different.

questions.prompt: Which command discards uncommitted edits to a tracked file permanently?
options: git stash
git restore file
git branch new
git commit -a
questions.explanation: git restore overwrites the working-tree file from the index/HEAD; stash and commit keep the edits.

questions.prompt: You run `git add .` in a folder that contains .env with API keys but no .gitignore. What is the right response before committing?
options: Commit it anyway, since private repositories are a safe place to keep API keys long term
Rename the file to .env.bak and commit it, since scanners only look for files named .env
Unstage it (git restore --staged .env), add it to .gitignore, and rotate the key if it was committed
Commit it, then delete the file in the next commit so the key disappears from history
questions.explanation: Anything committed stays in history; avoid committing, and revoke keys that were exposed.

questions.prompt: A result file records `dirty: true`. How many of your results from such runs should be trusted as reproducible from the commit alone? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: Dirty means the code differed from the recorded commit, so the commit id does not identify the code.

questions.prompt: Describe two checks that show a recorded result is reproducible from its commit, and one that shows it is not.
rubric: Fresh clone/checkout of the commit, rerun with the config and compare the numbers.
Confirm the dirty flag is false and the config in the result equals git show <commit>:config.
A mismatch, uncommitted data/dependency, or unseeded randomness indicates it is not reproducible.

rubric: git bisect start; git bisect bad (current); git bisect good <known-good-commit>.
git bisect run ./check.sh and read the reported first bad commit.
git bisect reset to return to the original branch.
